rationale: A wins because it interrogates the announcement instead of decorating it. Its best angle, "Substack says its top creators split more than $400M last year — and won't say how the split works," turns the company's own number into a reportable accountability story. B has useful bones, but "$400 million in creator earnings is an inconvenient number for the subscription fatigue narrative" manufactures a trend fight the fact block did not give it. That is how you turn a decent pitch into homework for the reporter.
gaps_in_A: "Substack has stopped competing with Mailchimp and started competing with YouTube" imports a competitive frame not supplied in the update; it works as shorthand, but it needs sourcing before it leaves the building.

"Video hosting is one of the most expensive infrastructure commitments a platform can make" is plausible, but still external context; A correctly demands proof, yet the angle leans on that cost claim early.

"the people who chose Substack precisely because it was text now face a feed that rewards something they didn't sign up to make" overstates pressure from an optional feature unless Substack can prove distribution now favors video.
gaps_in_B: "subscription fatigue discourse of the past few years" and "widely published since 2022–2023" are invented context. The update gives no prevailing belief, no trend line, and no comparison.
"implying $40M or more flowed to Substack from top creators alone" does arithmetic before defining whether $400M is gross, net, pre-fee, post-fee, or even all subject to the 10% cut.
"the broader debate over creator monetization models is active" is a fake news peg unless tied to a current, named story. It sounds like a pitch writer trying to borrow urgency from the wallpaper.
"what a specific writer with 10,000 paid subscribers should actually do Tuesday morning" invents a sample creator size. Harmless as color in a brainstorm, sloppy as an evidence-bound angle.
